query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, the wear resistance is governed by the uniform dispersion of fine TiC particles that refine the microstructure and increase hardness, thereby reducing wear loss.
generation.material_initial_state: An Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coating with little or no TiC reinforcement.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of TiC (e.g., varying between 10 wt.% to 30 wt.%) during laser cladding.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under consistent load, sliding speed, and environmental conditions typical of wear-resistant applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure in which finely dispersed TiC particles create a refined grain structure and act as obstacles to plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: TiC particles act as dispersion-strengthening agents that impede dislocation motion and crack propagation, enhancing the coating’s hardness and resistance to abrasive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: An optimal addition (around 20 wt.% TiC) will yield a predominantly single-phase BCC matrix with well-dispersed TiC reinforcements, resulting in increased hardness and lower wear loss compared to a baseline alloy without sufficient TiC dispersion.
generation.baseline: An Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 coating without added TiC or with insufficient TiC content to produce significant microstructural refinement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for TiC contents typically between 10 wt.% and 30 wt.% under standard wear test conditions; outside this range (e.g., excessive TiC leading to particle agglomeration, or under extreme wear conditions) other mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The influence of TiC particle size distribution and potential inhomogeneities on wear performance remains uncertain, and contributions from other phase transformations or reinforcement effects cannot be completely ruled out.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 coatings with varying TiC amounts (0%, 10%, 20%, 30%) using identical processing conditions. Test each coating using a standard pin-on-disk wear test while also measuring microhardness and microstructural characteristics (grain size and particle distribution) via microscopy.
measurements: Quantitative wear loss (mass loss or wear track depth)
Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase distribution, and TiC particle dispersion)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if coatings with the optimal TiC addition (around 20 wt.%) do not show a statistically significant improvement in hardness and reduction in wear loss compared to the baseline, or if no clear correlation between controlled TiC dispersion (refined microstructure) and wear performance is observed.

## Abstract
AbstractAl1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coatings with different TiC contents were prepared using laser cladding. The effect of TiC on the microstructure, hardness and wear resistance of the coatings was investigated. It was found that the phase structure of the coating with 10 wt.% TiC was a single BCC phase with no other precipitated phase. When 20 wt.% TiC was added, the phase structure of the coating was a BCC phase and TiC phase. When the TiC content increased to 30 wt.%, more TiC-reinforcing phase was formed. With the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was enhanced and the wear loss clearly decreased, which was closely related to the change in the coating structure. The addition of TiC to high-entropy alloys plays the role of fine-grain strengthening and dispersion strengthening.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, wear resistance, coatings, titanium carbide
